en.title: Biology: the whole course
en.short: What biology covers, how biology degrees are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: What biology is
sections.text:
Biology is the scientific study of living organisms and the systems they form. It ranges from molecules and cells to tissues, organs, whole organisms, populations and ecosystems. It asks how life works, how it varies, how it changes over time and how it interacts with the physical environment.

Biology overlaps with chemistry, physics, mathematics, geography and medicine, but it is not the same as medicine. It uses observation, controlled experiments, field studies, models and statistics. Because living systems are complex, biologists often combine several kinds of evidence before accepting a conclusion.

These summaries teach principles and standard methods. They do not replace your department’s handbook, laboratory rules or current safety guidance.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text:
Degree length and award names differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, a university BSc in Biology usually takes four years. Polytechnic students often take a National Diploma (ND) and then a Higher National Diploma (HND), commonly in science laboratory technology or applied biology, with industrial training. In the United Kingdom, a BSc usually takes three years, or four in Scotland; an integrated master’s usually adds a year. A taught master’s commonly takes one to two years full time, or longer part time, and usually includes a dissertation.

Early years usually cover the shared foundations: scientific method, chemistry, cell biology, genetics and ecology. Later years add physiology, microbiology, molecular biology, biotechnology and field or laboratory methods. Most programmes end with a supervised project. Exact module names, credit loads and training rules vary, so check your department’s handbook.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics build the base. Scientific method and biostatistics teach how to design studies and handle data. Chemistry of life covers water, pH and biological molecules. Cell structure and function introduces organelles and membranes. Enzymes and bioenergetics explain catalysis, energy and metabolism. The cell cycle, mitosis and meiosis lead into Mendelian genetics and inheritance. Molecular biology covers DNA, replication, transcription and translation. Evolution and natural selection give the unifying framework. Diversity and taxonomy survey living groups, and ecology foundations introduce organisms and their environments.

Core topics deepen the same themes. Biochemistry and metabolism extend bioenergetics. Molecular genetics and gene regulation explain how genes are controlled. Linkage, recombination and genomics show how genes are mapped and studied at scale. Microbiology covers bacteria, viruses and other microbes. Plant structure and physiology and animal physiology compare how organisms function. Developmental biology, immunology and ecology of populations, communities and ecosystems add whole-organism and group perspectives. Conservation biology, evolutionary biology and phylogenetics, biotechnology, bioinformatics, laboratory and field methods, ethics and biosafety, and a research project complete the core.

Master’s topics include advanced cell signalling and molecular biology, advanced ecology and evolutionary biology, systems biology and advanced bioinformatics, and research methods with a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study biology at several scales and keep linking them. When you learn a structure, ask what function it serves. When you learn a process, write it as a sequence with inputs, outputs and control points. Draw diagrams from memory and label them. For example, draw a cell or a food web from memory, then check.

Practise calculations in biostatistics, genetics and bioenergetics. Write the formula, substitute with units, and check whether the answer is reasonable. Learn the assumptions behind a statistical test before using it.

Use a laboratory or field notebook properly. Record what you did, what you observed and what you changed. Read the current textbook chapter before the class, then review it within a day. Use past questions to find gaps, not as a substitute for understanding.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Memorising words without understanding is the main mistake. Examiners often ask you to explain, compare or predict, not just define. Another common error is confusing similar pairs: mitosis and meiosis, transcription and translation, genotype and phenotype, or a population and a community.

Students also ignore statistics. A mean without a measure of spread, or a test used without checking its assumptions, can mislead. In calculations, missing units or mixing units causes wrong answers. In laboratory work, unsafe practice, poor labelling and copied results are serious.

Do not treat taxonomy or scientific ideas as fixed. Classification and accepted explanations change as evidence grows. Finally, read the question carefully. Many marks are lost by answering a nearby question instead of the one asked.

keyPoints: Biology studies life at scales from molecules and cells to organisms, populations and ecosystems.
Degree length and award names differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Learn each structure with its function and each process as a sequence of inputs, outputs and controls.
Practise calculations and check the assumptions behind statistical tests.
Confusing similar processes and ignoring units or statistics are common causes of lost marks.
Laboratory and field records must be honest, safe and clearly labelled.

en.title: Scientific method and biostatistics for biology
en.short: Design, descriptive statistics, probability, common tests, correlation and regression.

sections.heading: Designing experiments
sections.text: An experiment tests a hypothesis, a testable prediction. The null hypothesis H0 says there is no effect; the alternative H1 says there is. The independent variable is manipulated, the dependent variable is measured, and controlled variables are kept constant. A negative control receives no active treatment; a positive control receives a known effective treatment. Replication repeats measurements or independent units, reducing chance variation. Sampling should be random and representative, with enough units and a stated method, because biased samples cannot be rescued by statistics.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text: Descriptive statistics summarise a sample. The mean is Σx ÷ n; the median is the middle value; the mode is the most frequent. Range, variance and standard deviation measure spread. For a sample, variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1) and standard deviation s = √s². Example: leaf lengths 10, 12, 11, 13, 14 mm. Mean = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 mm. Squared deviations total 10. s² = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 mm², so s = √2.5 = 1.58 mm.

sections.heading: Probability and tests
sections.text: Probability describes chance. For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed if H0 is true. Choose a significance level α before testing, often 0.05; reject H0 when p < α. Common tests include the t-test for two means, ANOVA for three or more means, and chi-square for counts: χ² = Σ((O − E)² ÷ E). Check assumptions such as independence and normality. A non-significant result does not prove H0.

sections.heading: Relationships and meaning
sections.text: Correlation measures the strength and direction of association. Pearson r runs from −1 to +1; r near 0 means little linear association. Regression fits y = a + bx to predict y from x. Correlation is not causation: a third variable or study design may explain the link. Report effect size, confidence intervals and sample size, and interpret results in biological context, not by p-values alone.

keyPoints: A hypothesis test compares data with H0; reject H0 when p < α, and remember p is not the probability that H0 is true.
Independent variables are manipulated, dependent variables measured, and controlled variables kept constant; include negative and positive controls where appropriate.
Replication and random, representative sampling reduce chance variation and bias; sample size and sampling method must be reported.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; sample standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).
The t-test compares two means, ANOVA compares three or more means, and chi-square tests counts with χ² = Σ((O − E)² ÷ E).
Correlation measures linear association and regression predicts y from x, but correlation does not prove causation; report effect size and confidence intervals.

en.title: Chemistry of life: water, pH and biological molecules
en.short: Water’s properties, pH and buffers, chemical bonds, and the four main biological molecules.

sections.heading: Water and bonds
sections.text:
Water is polar: oxygen carries a partial negative charge, each hydrogen a partial positive charge. This lets water molecules form hydrogen bonds, weak attractions between the hydrogen of one molecule and the oxygen of another. Hydrogen bonds explain water’s high boiling point, high specific heat capacity, surface tension and its solvent power for ions and polar molecules. Non-polar substances such as fats do not dissolve.

Covalent bonds share electrons and are strong; ionic bonds transfer them. Hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces are weak alone but numerous, and they shape proteins and DNA.

sections.heading: pH and buffers
sections.text:
pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], where [H⁺] is the hydrogen ion concentration in mol/dm³. One pH unit means a tenfold change in [H⁺]. Example: 0.01 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid dissociates fully, so [H⁺] = 10⁻² mol/dm³ and pH = 2.

A buffer resists pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added. It is usually a weak acid mixed with its conjugate base, or a weak base with its conjugate acid. The carbonic acid and bicarbonate pair buffers blood near pH 7.4.

sections.heading: Carbohydrates and lipids
sections.text:
Carbohydrates have the general formula (CH₂O)n. Monosaccharides such as glucose are single units; disaccharides such as sucrose are two joined units; polysaccharides such as starch, glycogen and cellulose are long chains. They serve as fuel and structure.

Lipids are mostly non-polar and insoluble in water. Triglycerides are glycerol plus three fatty acids and store energy densely. Phospholipids form cell membranes. Steroids include cholesterol, a membrane component, and hormones that act as signalling molecules.

sections.heading: Proteins and nucleic acids
sections.text:
Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. The sequence is the primary structure; folding into alpha helices and beta sheets is secondary; the overall three-dimensional shape is tertiary; several chains give quaternary structure. Shape determines function, and heat or extreme pH can denature a protein.

Nucleic acids are chains of nucleotides, each with a sugar, a phosphate and a base. DNA stores information in its base sequence; RNA carries and interprets it.

keyPoints: Water is polar and forms hydrogen bonds, giving it a high specific heat capacity, high surface tension and strong solvent power.
pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]; each pH unit is a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.
A buffer is a weak acid with its conjugate base, or a weak base with its conjugate acid, and it resists pH change.
Carbohydrates follow (CH₂O)n, lipids are mostly non-polar, proteins are amino acid chains and nucleic acids are nucleotide chains.
Protein function depends on three-dimensional shape, which heat or extreme pH can destroy by denaturation.

en.title: Cell structure and function
en.short: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, membranes, organelles, cytoskeleton, junctions and microscopy.

sections.heading: Cell types
sections.text: Cells are the basic units of life. Prokaryotic cells, the bacteria and archaea, have no membrane-bound nucleus. Their DNA lies in a nucleoid, and they lack membrane-bound organelles; their ribosomes are smaller than eukaryotic ribosomes. Eukaryotic cells, found in protists, fungi, plants and animals, have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. A bacterium is usually a few micrometres across, while many animal cells are larger, often tens of micrometres across.

sections.heading: Membranes and transport
sections.text: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins. It is selectively permeable: some substances cross freely, others need help. Diffusion and facilitated diffusion move substances down a concentration gradient without ATP. Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one. Active transport uses ATP and carrier proteins to move substances against a gradient. Endocytosis and exocytosis move material in vesicles. Case: a red blood cell in distilled water swells and may burst; in strong salt solution it shrinks.

sections.heading: Organelles and cytoskeleton
sections.text: Organelles divide labour. The nucleus stores DNA. Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration. Chloroplasts in plants and algae carry out photosynthesis. Rough endoplasmic reticulum, studded with ribosomes, makes proteins; smooth endoplasmic reticulum makes lipids. The Golgi apparatus modifies and sorts proteins and lipids. Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes. Ribosomes make proteins. The cytoskeleton is a network of microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules. It supports the cell, maintains shape, moves materials and enables cell movement.

sections.heading: Junctions and microscopy
sections.text: Animal cells join by tight junctions, which seal gaps; desmosomes, which anchor cells; and gap junctions, which let ions and small molecules pass. Plant cells connect through plasmodesmata. Microscopy depends on magnification and resolution. Magnification enlarges an image; resolution is the smallest distance at which two points can be seen separately. A light microscope resolves about 0.2 micrometres and can show living cells. Electron microscopes resolve finer detail but usually need fixed, dead specimens. Transmission electron microscopy shows internal structure; scanning electron microscopy shows surfaces. Stains improve contrast.

keyPoints: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes have both.
The plasma membrane is a selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer.
Diffusion and osmosis are passive; active transport uses ATP.
Organelles divide labour, and the cytoskeleton supports and moves the cell.
Tight junctions, desmosomes and gap junctions connect animal cells; plasmodesmata connect plant cells.
Resolution, not magnification alone, limits what a microscope can show.

en.title: Enzymes and bioenergetics
en.short: Enzyme kinetics and inhibition, ATP and redox, glycolysis, respiration and photosynthesis.

sections.heading: Enzyme kinetics
sections.text: Enzymes are protein catalysts that lower activation energy without changing the equilibrium. In the Michaelis-Menten model, v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S]). Vmax is the maximum rate when enzyme is saturated. Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax; a low Km means high apparent affinity. Reaction rate rises with substrate concentration and then levels off. Enzyme activity depends on pH and temperature.

sections.heading: Inhibition and example
sections.text: Competitive inhibitors bind the active site and raise apparent Km; Vmax is unchanged. Noncompetitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and lower Vmax. Example: Vmax = 100 µmol/min, Km = 2 mM, [S] = 3 mM. v = 100 × 3 ÷ (2 + 3) = 60 µmol/min. At [S] = 10 mM, v = 100 × 10 ÷ 12 = 83.3 µmol/min.

sections.heading: ATP and redox
sections.text: ATP is the cell’s main energy currency. Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate releases free energy, which drives endergonic reactions when the two are coupled. Redox reactions transfer electrons. Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain. NAD+ and FAD accept electrons to form NADH and FADH2, which carry reducing power to the electron transport chain.

sections.heading: Energy pathways
sections.text: Glycolysis breaks one glucose into two pyruvate in the cytosol, with a net gain of 2 ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation and 2 NADH from oxidation steps. Aerobic respiration oxidises pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, runs the citric acid cycle, and uses the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis to make much more ATP, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor. Photosynthesis reverses the energy flow: light reactions in thylakoids split water, release O2 and make ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle in the stroma uses them to fix CO2 into sugar.

keyPoints: Enzymes lower activation energy and do not change reaction equilibrium.
Michaelis-Menten rate: v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S]); Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax.
Competitive inhibition raises apparent Km; pure noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax.
ATP hydrolysis to ADP and phosphate releases free energy for coupled reactions.
Glycolysis gives net 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose and produces 2 pyruvate.
Aerobic respiration uses the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis; photosynthesis uses light reactions and the Calvin cycle.

en.title: Cell cycle, mitosis and meiosis
en.short: The cell cycle and its checkpoints, mitosis, meiosis and the origins of genetic variation.

sections.heading: Cell cycle and control
sections.text:
The cell cycle is the sequence from one cell division to the next. Interphase has G1 (growth), S (DNA replication) and G2 (preparation). M phase is mitosis and cytokinesis. DNA content doubles in S, but chromosome number stays the same because sister chromatids share one centromere.

Control uses checkpoints, especially at G1/S and G2/M, and the spindle checkpoint. Cyclins bind cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) to drive the cycle. A checkpoint pauses the cycle if DNA is damaged or chromosomes are unattached. Loss of control can lead to cancer.

sections.heading: Mitosis
sections.text: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid (two chromosome sets) cells. In prophase chromosomes condense and the spindle forms. In metaphase chromosomes line up at the equator. In anaphase sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles. In telophase nuclei reform, and cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm. Example: a human somatic cell has 46 chromosomes. After S phase it has 46 chromosomes, each with two chromatids. Mitosis gives two cells with 46 chromosomes each.

sections.heading: Meiosis
sections.text: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and occurs in two divisions. In meiosis I, homologous chromosomes pair and crossing over exchanges segments in prophase I. In metaphase I homologues line up in pairs; in anaphase I they separate. Each daughter cell is haploid (one chromosome set) but its chromosomes have two chromatids. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, like mitosis. Example: human 2n = 46. Meiosis I gives two cells with 23 chromosomes; meiosis II gives four haploid cells with 23 chromosomes each. In human males all four become sperm; in females one becomes the ovum and the others polar bodies.

sections.heading: Variation in sexual reproduction
sections.text: Sexual reproduction creates variation in three ways. Crossing over in prophase I makes new combinations of alleles (gene variants) on a chromosome. Independent assortment in metaphase I gives many possible combinations of maternal and paternal homologues. Random fertilisation combines one gamete from each parent. Mutation is the original source of new alleles. These processes explain why siblings differ, except identical twins.

keyPoints: The cell cycle has interphase (G1, S, G2) and M phase; DNA replicates in S while chromosome number stays the same.
Cyclin-CDK complexes and checkpoints control progress through the cycle.
Mitosis separates sister chromatids and produces two genetically identical diploid cells.
Meiosis has two divisions: meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes and meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
Crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation are the main sources of genetic variation in sexual reproduction.
In humans, diploid cells have 46 chromosomes and haploid gametes have 23.

en.title: Mendelian genetics and inheritance
en.short: Mendel’s laws, monohybrid and dihybrid crosses, probability, pedigrees, codominance and sex linkage.

sections.heading: Mendel’s laws and monohybrid crosses
sections.text:
A gene is a length of DNA coding for a trait; its variants are alleles. Homozygous means two identical alleles, heterozygous two different ones. Genotype is the allele pair, phenotype the visible trait.

Mendel’s law of segregation: the two alleles separate in meiosis, so each gamete carries one. A monohybrid cross Aa × Aa gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, a 3:1 phenotype ratio. A test cross with a homozygous recessive reveals an unknown genotype: Aa × aa gives 1 Aa : 1 aa, while AA × aa gives all Aa.

sections.heading: Dihybrid crosses and probability
sections.text:
Law of independent assortment: alleles of two genes on different chromosomes go to gametes independently. A dihybrid cross RrYy × RrYy gives the phenotype ratio 9:3:3:1.

A Punnett square lists the gametes and their combinations. For independent events, multiply probabilities. In RrYy × RrYy the chance of rr is 1/4 and of yy is 1/4, so the chance of rryy is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16, one part of the sixteen in that ratio.

sections.heading: Pedigrees
sections.text:
A pedigree is a family tree of inheritance. Squares are males, circles females, filled symbols affected people; horizontal lines join mates, vertical lines show descent.

Clues: an affected child of two unaffected parents suggests a recessive allele. An affected father passing the trait to all daughters and no sons suggests X-linked dominant inheritance. A pedigree suggests a mode of inheritance; it does not prove one.

sections.heading: Extensions of Mendel’s ratios
sections.text:
In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is intermediate: red × white snapdragon gives pink, and the F2 is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. In codominance both alleles are fully expressed, as in blood group AB.

Multiple alleles means more than two alleles exist in a population, though each person carries two. The ABO group has three: IA, IB and i.

Sex linkage: genes carried on the X chromosome. Males have one X, so one recessive allele is enough; X-linked recessive conditions such as haemophilia are commoner in males.

keyPoints: Law of segregation: the two alleles of a gene separate in meiosis, so each gamete carries one.
Aa × Aa gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, a 3:1 phenotype ratio.
Independent assortment applies to genes on different chromosomes; RrYy × RrYy gives 9:3:3:1.
Multiply probabilities for independent events: rryy from RrYy × RrYy is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.
A pedigree suggests a mode of inheritance but does not prove it.
Incomplete dominance gives an intermediate heterozygote, codominance expresses both alleles, and X-linked recessive traits appear more often in males.

en.title: Molecular biology: DNA, replication, transcription and translation
en.short: DNA structure and replication, transcription and RNA processing, translation and the genetic code, and mutation.

sections.heading: DNA structure and replication
sections.text:
DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands, which run in opposite directions, with a sugar-phosphate backbone. Bases A, T, G and C project inward. A pairs with T by two hydrogen bonds; G pairs with C by three. The base sequence carries information.

Replication is semi-conservative: each new molecule keeps one old strand. Helicase unwinds DNA. Primase makes an RNA primer. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the 3' end, reading the template 3' to 5'. The leading strand grows continuously; the lagging strand forms Okazaki fragments, joined by DNA ligase. Proofreading limits errors.

sections.heading: Transcription and RNA processing
sections.text:
Transcription copies a gene into RNA. RNA polymerase binds a promoter, unwinds DNA and adds nucleotides 5' to 3' while reading the template 3' to 5'. Only one strand is the template. In bacteria, transcription and translation can occur together.

In eukaryotes, transcription occurs in the nucleus and makes pre-mRNA. RNA processing adds a 5' cap and poly-A tail, and splicing removes introns and joins exons. mRNA leaves the nucleus.

sections.heading: Translation and genetic code
sections.text:
Translation builds a polypeptide on a ribosome. Each mRNA codon is three bases. A tRNA carries one amino acid and has an anticodon that pairs with the codon. AUG is the start codon and sets the reading frame. UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons. The ribosome joins amino acids by peptide bonds.

The genetic code is triplet, non-overlapping and degenerate: most amino acids have more than one codon. It is nearly universal.

sections.heading: Mutation
sections.text:
A mutation is a change in DNA sequence. A substitution replaces one base. An insertion or deletion adds or removes bases; unless the number is a multiple of three, it causes a frameshift and changes codons.

A silent mutation changes a codon but not the amino acid, because the code is degenerate. A missense mutation changes one amino acid. A nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon. Frameshifts destroy function. In beta-globin, GAG changes to GTG, so mRNA becomes GUG and glutamate becomes valine, causing sickle-cell haemoglobin.

keyPoints: DNA is antiparallel and double-stranded; A pairs with T and G pairs with C.
Replication is semi-conservative and DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the 3' end.
Transcription makes RNA 5' to 3'; eukaryotes process pre-mRNA by capping, poly-A tail addition and splicing.
Translation uses mRNA codons, tRNA anticodons and ribosomes; AUG starts and UAA, UAG, UGA stop.
The genetic code is triplet, non-overlapping and degenerate.
Substitutions can be silent, missense or nonsense; insertions or deletions may cause frameshifts.

en.title: Evolution and natural selection
en.short: This summary covers evidence for evolution, natural selection, adaptation, speciation, allele frequencies and the Hardy-Weinberg principle.

sections.heading: Evidence for evolution
sections.text: Evolution is change in the heritable characteristics of a population over generations. Evidence comes from independent sources: fossils showing transitional forms, comparative anatomy such as homologous limbs, molecular sequences revealing shared ancestry, and observed population changes such as antibiotic resistance in bacteria. These support common descent and descent with modification. The theory does not rest on one fossil or one experiment.

sections.heading: Natural selection and adaptation
sections.text: Natural selection acts when individuals vary, the variation is heritable, and some variants leave more offspring because of their environment. Those variants become more common. Fitness means relative reproductive success in a given environment, not strength. An adaptation is a heritable trait that improves fitness there; the word also names the process producing it. Selection can be directional, stabilising or disruptive. It acts on phenotypes, but only heritable differences pass on.

sections.heading: Speciation
sections.text: A species is often defined as a group of populations whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring, though this biological species concept does not fit all organisms. Speciation is the formation of new species, usually after reproductive isolation. In allopatric speciation a geographic barrier separates populations. In sympatric speciation isolation arises without a barrier, for example through polyploidy in plants. Mutation, selection, genetic drift (chance change in allele frequencies) and isolation then build differences.

sections.heading: Allele frequencies and Hardy-Weinberg
sections.text: An allele frequency is the proportion of all copies of a gene in a population that are a particular allele. For two alleles, p + q = 1. The Hardy-Weinberg principle says that in an ideal population with random mating, no selection, no mutation, no migration and large size, allele and genotype frequencies stay constant. Expected genotypes are p², 2pq and q², so p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Example: if q = 0.2, then p = 0.8. Expected affected homozygotes q² = 0.04, carriers 2pq = 0.32, and unaffected homozygotes p² = 0.64. In 500 people that is 20 affected and 160 carriers. Real populations often depart from these assumptions.

keyPoints: Evolution is change in heritable characteristics of populations over generations, supported by fossils, comparative anatomy, molecular data and observed change.
Natural selection needs heritable variation and differences in reproductive success; fitness is relative in a given environment.
Adaptation is both a heritable trait that raises fitness and the process that produces it.
Speciation usually follows reproductive isolation, often geographic (allopatric) or without a barrier (sympatric).
Allele frequency is the proportion of gene copies that are a given allele; for two alleles p + q = 1.
Hardy-Weinberg: with random mating and no selection, mutation, migration or genetic drift, genotypes are p², 2pq and q², and p² + 2pq + q² = 1.

en.title: Diversity of life and taxonomy
en.short: Classification, binomial names, phylogenetic trees, and the main groups of life.

sections.heading: Naming and ranking
sections.text: Taxonomy is the science of describing and classifying organisms. It uses a hierarchy of ranks: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. A species is the basic unit; its name is binomial. In binomial nomenclature, the genus name is capitalised and the species epithet is lower case, and the whole name is italicised (or underlined in handwriting). Example: Homo sapiens and Panthera leo. Names are tied to type specimens and governed by codes that differ for animals, plants and bacteria. Classification is a hypothesis.

sections.heading: Reading phylogenetic trees
sections.text: A phylogenetic tree is a diagram of evolutionary relationships. Each branching point (node) represents a common ancestor; the tips are present-day taxa. A clade is a group containing an ancestor and all its descendants. Trees are built from shared derived characters (homologies), not from overall similarity, because convergent evolution can produce similar features in unrelated groups. Example: birds and crocodiles are more closely related to each other than to lizards, so they form a clade. Rotating branches at a node does not change relationships.

sections.heading: Viruses and prokaryotes
sections.text: Viruses are acellular: a nucleic acid core (DNA or RNA) inside a protein capsid, sometimes with a lipid envelope. They have no metabolism and reproduce only inside host cells, so they are not placed in the tree of cellular life. Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes: no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles. Bacteria usually have peptidoglycan in their cell walls; archaea lack it and have branched ether-linked membrane lipids. Many archaea live in extreme environments. "Prokaryote" describes a grade, not a clade.

sections.heading: Eukaryotic diversity
sections.text: Protists are a loose, mostly unicellular group of eukaryotes; the term is convenient but not a clade. Fungi are heterotrophs with chitin cell walls that absorb nutrients, usually as filamentous hyphae. Plants are multicellular photosynthetic organisms with cellulose walls and alternation of generations. Animals are multicellular heterotrophs without cell walls, usually with tissues and a diploid life cycle. These four groups are distinguished by cell wall, nutrition and body form.

keyPoints: Taxonomy uses a ranked hierarchy and binomial names: genus capitalised, species lower case, both italicised.
A phylogenetic tree shows evolutionary relationships; a clade is an ancestor plus all its descendants.
Trees are built from shared derived characters, not overall similarity.
Viruses are acellular and reproduce only inside host cells, so they are outside the cellular tree of life.
Bacteria usually have peptidoglycan cell walls; archaea lack it and have ether-linked membrane lipids.
Protists are a mixed group, not a clade; fungi absorb nutrients through chitin walls, plants have cellulose walls, and animals lack cell walls.

en.title: Principles of ecology
en.short: Organisms and their environment, populations, species interactions, communities, ecosystems and biomes.

sections.heading: Organisms and environment
sections.text: Ecology studies how organisms interact with each other and with their surroundings. The environment has abiotic factors, such as light, temperature, water and soil, and biotic factors, such as food and predators. Each species tolerates a range of conditions; outside that range it cannot survive. Its niche is its role and the resources it uses. A habitat is where it lives.

sections.heading: Populations
sections.text:
A population is a group of one species in one area. Its size changes through births, deaths, immigration and emigration. Exponential growth is dN/dt = rN, where r is the intrinsic growth rate. Logistic growth adds a limit: dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), where K is the carrying capacity, the maximum number the environment can support. Growth slows as N approaches K. Populations are regulated by density-dependent factors, such as competition and disease, and density-independent factors, such as drought and fire.

Example: with r = 0.2 per year, N = 50 and K = 500:
exponential growth = 0.2 × 50 = 10 individuals per year
logistic growth = 0.2 × 50 × (1 − 50 ÷ 500) = 9 individuals per year

sections.heading: Species and communities
sections.text: Species interactions include competition, predation, herbivory, parasitism, mutualism and commensalism. Competition can limit both species; predation can control prey numbers. A community is all the populations living together. Its structure includes species richness (the number of species), evenness (how similar their abundances are) and trophic levels. Succession is the change in community composition over time.

sections.heading: Ecosystems and biomes
sections.text: An ecosystem is a community plus its physical environment. Energy enters mainly as sunlight and flows through producers, consumers and decomposers; only a small fraction, often around 10%, passes to the next trophic level, and the exact value varies. Matter cycles: carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and water move between organisms and the environment. Climate and soil determine major biomes, such as tropical rainforest, savanna, desert, temperate grassland, temperate forest, taiga and tundra; aquatic biomes are also recognised.

keyPoints: Ecology studies interactions between organisms and their abiotic and biotic environment.
Exponential growth is dN/dt = rN; logistic growth is dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), where K is carrying capacity.
Populations are regulated by density-dependent and density-independent factors.
Species interactions include competition, predation, herbivory, parasitism, mutualism and commensalism.
Community structure includes species richness, evenness and trophic levels.
Energy flows through ecosystems and matter cycles; climate and soil shape major biomes.

en.title: Biochemistry and metabolism: pathways and regulation
en.short: Glycolysis, TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, photosynthesis and metabolic integration.

sections.heading: Glycolysis and TCA
sections.text:
Glycolysis converts one glucose to two pyruvate in the cytosol, with net gain of 2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation (direct ATP synthesis) and 2 NADH. Pyruvate dehydrogenase oxidises pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, releasing CO2 and forming NADH. The tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle oxidises acetyl-CoA to CO2; per turn it gives 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP.

Worked example: one glucose gives two acetyl-CoA. Two TCA turns give 2 × 3 = 6 NADH, 2 × 1 = 2 FADH2 and 2 × 1 = 2 GTP. Add glycolysis: 2 NADH and 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH from pyruvate dehydrogenase. ATP totals from NADH and FADH2 vary by shuttle and textbook; use your course’s convention.

sections.heading: Oxidative phosphorylation
sections.text: NADH and FADH2 feed electrons to the electron transport chain. Electron transfer pumps protons, creating a proton motive force. ATP synthase uses this force to make ATP by chemiosmosis. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water. In photosynthesis, light reactions split water, release oxygen, and make ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar, catalysed by rubisco.

sections.heading: Regulation
sections.text: Pathways are controlled by allosteric regulation (effectors bind away from the active site), covalent modification and hormone signals. Phosphofructokinase-1, the main glycolysis control point, is inhibited by ATP and citrate and activated by AMP, ADP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. Pyruvate dehydrogenase is inhibited by acetyl-CoA and NADH. Isocitrate dehydrogenase is activated by ADP and inhibited by ATP and NADH. Feedback matches flux to energy charge and demand.

sections.heading: Metabolic integration
sections.text: Insulin and glucagon switch fed and fasting pathways. In the fed state, excess glucose becomes glycogen and fat; acetyl-CoA from carbohydrate and fatty acid beta-oxidation enters the TCA cycle. In fasting, glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis supply glucose, while lipolysis releases fatty acids and liver makes ketone bodies. Amino acids are deaminated; carbon skeletons enter glycolysis or the TCA cycle, and nitrogen enters the urea cycle. Animals cannot convert acetyl-CoA to glucose: pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible.

keyPoints: Per glucose, glycolysis gives net 2 ATP and 2 NADH; two TCA turns give 6 NADH, 2 FADH2 and 2 GTP.
ATP yield from NADH and FADH2 depends on the shuttle and textbook convention.
Oxidative phosphorylation uses a proton motive force and ATP synthase, with oxygen as final electron acceptor.
Photosynthesis light reactions make ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle fixes CO2.
Phosphofructokinase-1 is inhibited by ATP and citrate and activated by AMP, ADP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.
Insulin and glucagon switch storage and mobilisation, and animals cannot convert acetyl-CoA to glucose.

en.title: Molecular genetics and gene regulation
en.short: Gene structure and expression, transcription factors, operons, chromatin, RNA processing, ncRNAs and DNA repair.

sections.heading: Gene structure
sections.text: Prokaryotic genes are usually continuous, with a promoter, a transcribed region and a terminator. Related genes often sit in one operon and are transcribed together. Eukaryotic genes are usually split into exons (coding or retained sequences) and introns (removed by splicing). Each has its own promoter and often distant enhancers. Eukaryotic transcription happens in the nucleus and is separated from translation, which happens in the cytoplasm.

sections.heading: Transcription factors and operons
sections.text: Transcription factors are proteins that bind DNA or other factors to activate or repress transcription. General factors help RNA polymerase start; specific factors control particular genes. An operon is a set of co-transcribed genes controlled by one regulatory region. In the lac operon of Escherichia coli, the repressor LacI blocks transcription when lactose is absent. When lactose (actually allolactose) binds LacI, the repressor leaves and the genes are expressed. CAP also activates the operon when glucose is low. This is a case of negative and positive control.

sections.heading: Chromatin and RNA processing
sections.text: Eukaryotic DNA is wrapped around histones to form chromatin. Methylation of cytosine in DNA and modification of histone tails (acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation) can open or close chromatin. These epigenetic marks help regulate gene expression and can be inherited through cell division, though not always. RNA processing includes 5′ capping, 3′ polyadenylation and splicing. Alternative splicing lets one gene make several mRNAs. In prokaryotes, transcription and translation are coupled and there is little processing.

sections.heading: Non-coding RNA and repair
sections.text: Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) are RNAs that are not translated. They include ribosomal RNA and transfer RNA, and regulatory RNAs such as microRNAs, which bind target mRNAs and reduce their expression, and long non-coding RNAs, which can guide chromatin changes. Mutation is a change in DNA sequence. Point mutations include substitutions, insertions and deletions; insertions or deletions not in multiples of three shift the reading frame. DNA repair systems, such as base excision repair, nucleotide excision repair and mismatch repair, correct damage. Unrepaired damage can cause disease.

keyPoints: Prokaryotic genes are often in operons and are transcribed with little RNA processing; eukaryotic genes have introns and are processed in the nucleus.
Transcription factors and operons control when genes are expressed; the lac operon uses both negative and positive control.
Chromatin modifications and DNA methylation regulate access to genes and can be inherited.
RNA processing includes capping, polyadenylation and splicing; alternative splicing increases protein diversity.
Non-coding RNAs regulate gene expression at several levels.
Mutations change DNA sequence; repair systems correct damage, and frameshift mutations change the reading frame.

en.title: Genetics: linkage, recombination and genomics
en.short: Linkage maps, sex determination, extranuclear and quantitative genetics, genomes and sequencing.

sections.heading: Linkage and mapping
sections.text:
Genes close together on one chromosome tend to be inherited together: they are linked. Crossing over in meiosis produces recombinants. Recombination frequency (RF) is the proportion of recombinant offspring; 1 map unit, or centimorgan (cM), equals 1 per cent recombination. RF underestimates the distance between distant loci, because double crossovers restore parental combinations, so three-point crosses are used.

Example: a testcross AaBb × aabb gives 1000 offspring: 430 AB, 420 ab, 75 Ab, 75 aB. Recombinants = 75 + 75 = 150, so RF = 150 ÷ 1000 = 0.15, that is 15 cM.

sections.heading: Sex and extranuclear genes
sections.text:
Sex may be set by chromosomes: in mammals XX is female and XY male; in birds ZW is female and ZZ male; in bees unfertilised eggs become haploid males. Temperature decides sex in some reptiles.

Extranuclear genes sit in mitochondria and chloroplasts. They are usually inherited from one parent only, often the mother, and can be heteroplasmic, meaning a cell holds a mixture of normal and mutant copies. They segregate randomly at cell division, so their inheritance is not Mendelian.

sections.heading: Quantitative genetics
sections.text:
Continuous traits such as height are usually polygenic and also shaped by environment. Phenotypic variance VP divides into genetic VG and environmental VE. Broad-sense heritability H² = VG ÷ VP; narrow-sense h² = VA ÷ VP uses only additive variance and predicts selection response R = h²S, where S is the selection differential.

Example: S = 2.0 cm and h² = 0.30 give R = 0.30 × 2.0 = 0.60 cm per generation. Heritability describes a population in a given environment, not a trait in general.

sections.heading: Genomes and sequencing
sections.text: Genome size and gene number do not rise together, the C-value paradox; much of a eukaryotic genome is non-coding: introns, repeats and transposons. Sanger sequencing stops synthesis with dideoxynucleotides; high-throughput methods read millions of short fragments at once. Overlapping reads assemble into contigs and scaffolds, and depth of coverage indicates reliability. Annotation finds genes from open reading frames, splice sites, homology and RNA evidence; predictions stay provisional until tested.

keyPoints: Linked genes lie on the same chromosome; recombination frequency = recombinants ÷ total offspring, and 1 cM = 1 per cent recombination.
Two-point map distances underestimate long distances because double crossovers restore parental combinations.
Sex can be chromosomal (XX/XY or ZZ/ZW) or set by environment; extranuclear genes are usually maternally inherited and can be heteroplasmic.
Broad-sense heritability H² = VG ÷ VP; narrow-sense h² = VA ÷ VP; response to selection R = h²S.
Eukaryotic genomes contain much non-coding DNA, so genome size does not track gene number.
Sequencing reads are assembled into contigs, and annotation predictions need experimental evidence.

en.title: Microbiology: cells, viruses and control
en.short: Bacterial and archaeal cells, viruses, growth, control, genetics and host interactions.

sections.heading: Prokaryote cell biology
sections.text:
Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes: single cells with no membrane-bound nucleus. Their DNA lies in a nucleoid, and they have 70S ribosomes. Bacteria have peptidoglycan cell walls; archaea lack peptidoglycan and have ether-linked membrane lipids, while bacteria use ester links.

Some bacteria form endospores (for example Bacillus and Clostridium), dormant forms that resist heat and drying. Plasmids are small extra DNA molecules. Flagella, pili and capsules help movement, attachment and protection.

sections.heading: Viral structure and replication
sections.text:
Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites: they have no metabolism and cannot reproduce outside a host cell. A virus has a nucleic acid genome (DNA or RNA, single or double stranded) inside a protein capsid, sometimes wrapped in an envelope.

Replication follows attachment, entry, uncoating, synthesis of components, assembly and release. Bacteriophages may be lytic, bursting the host, or lysogenic, when the genome integrates as a prophage.

sections.heading: Growth, metabolism and control
sections.text:
Growth is by binary fission. A batch culture passes through lag, log (exponential), stationary and death phases. Generation time is the doubling time. Example: 100 cells with a 30 min generation time after 3 h (6 doublings) give 100 × 2⁶ = 6,400 cells.

Metabolism varies: autotrophs fix CO₂, heterotrophs need organic carbon; aerobes use O₂, anaerobes do not. Sterilisation kills all microbes; disinfection reduces pathogens on surfaces. Autoclaving uses steam at 121 °C (about 15 psi) for 15 minutes. Antibiotics target bacterial structures; resistance arises by mutation or gene transfer.

sections.heading: Genetics, hosts and applications
sections.text:
Horizontal gene transfer spreads traits: transformation (uptake of free DNA), transduction (by phage) and conjugation (plasmid transfer between cells joined by a pilus).

Host-microbe interactions range from mutualism, such as gut bacteria, to pathogenicity. Virulence factors include toxins and adhesins. Normal microbiota compete with pathogens. Applied microbiology includes fermentation, antibiotic production, bioremediation and water treatment.

keyPoints: Bacteria have peptidoglycan walls; archaea lack peptidoglycan and have ether-linked lipids.
Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites with a nucleic acid genome inside a capsid.
Batch growth has lag, log, stationary and death phases; generation time is the doubling time.
Cell number after n doublings = initial number × 2ⁿ.
Sterilisation kills all microbes; autoclaving uses steam at 121 °C and about 15 psi for 15 minutes.
Horizontal gene transfer occurs by transformation, transduction and conjugation.

en.title: Plant structure and physiology
en.short: Plant anatomy, water and sugar transport, whole-plant photosynthesis, hormones, growth, reproduction and stress.

sections.heading: Plant body and transport
sections.text:
Angiosperms have roots, stems and leaves. Xylem carries water and minerals upward; its tracheids and vessel elements are dead at maturity. Phloem carries sugars; its sieve tube elements are living but lose their nucleus.

Water moves by water potential, ψ = ψs + ψp (solute potential plus pressure potential), from higher ψ to lower ψ. Example: ψs = −0.6 MPa and ψp = 0.2 MPa give ψ = −0.4 MPa; a leaf at −0.8 MPa draws water from the root.

Transpiration lowers leaf ψ and pulls water up the xylem. Cohesion and adhesion keep the column continuous (cohesion-tension theory). Root pressure acts mainly at night.

sections.heading: Photosynthesis in the plant
sections.text:
Leaves intercept light; mesophyll chloroplasts fix CO2. C3 plants make a three-carbon first product; C4 plants separate initial fixation from the Calvin cycle in space, and CAM plants in time. These adaptations reduce photorespiration, the wasteful fixation of oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, in hot, dry conditions.

Whole-plant photosynthesis depends on leaf area, light, CO2, water and nutrients. Stomata admit CO2 but lose water. Sucrose moves from source leaves, which export sugar, to sink tissues, which import it, through phloem loading and unloading.

sections.heading: Hormones and growth
sections.text:
Plant hormones are signalling molecules active at very low concentrations. Auxin promotes cell elongation and apical dominance; cytokinins promote cell division; gibberellins promote stem elongation and seed germination; abscisic acid (ABA) closes stomata and maintains dormancy; ethylene promotes ripening and senescence.

Growth is irreversible increase in size; development includes differentiation and morphogenesis. Phototropism and gravitropism guide shoots and roots. Flowering in many species depends on photoperiod or vernalization, a period of cold that makes the plant competent to flower.

sections.heading: Reproduction and stress
sections.text:
Angiosperms reproduce sexually. Flowers typically contain stamens and carpels; pollination transfers pollen, and double fertilisation forms embryo and endosperm. Seeds disperse and may remain dormant until conditions suit germination.

Stress responses include stomatal closure, osmotic adjustment and antioxidant defence. Drought and salinity lower water potential; ABA signals stomatal closure. Flooding limits oxygen, and heat damages proteins. Plants acclimate within limits; responses vary by species and habitat.

keyPoints: Xylem carries water and minerals in dead tracheids and vessel elements; phloem carries sugars in living sieve tube elements.
Water potential is ψ = ψs + ψp, and water moves from higher ψ to lower ψ.
Transpiration pulls water up the xylem by cohesion and adhesion, the cohesion-tension theory.
Whole-plant photosynthesis depends on leaf area, light, CO2, water and nutrients, and on source-to-sink transport.
Auxin, cytokinin, gibberellin, ABA and ethylene control growth, development and stress responses at very low concentrations.
Drought and salinity lower water potential; ABA closes stomata, while flooding and heat cause oxygen shortage and protein damage.

en.title: Animal physiology: homeostasis and comparative systems
en.short: Homeostasis and animal physiology: nerve, hormone, muscle, circulation, respiration, excretion, digestion and reproduction.

sections.heading: Homeostasis and control
sections.text:
Homeostasis keeps internal conditions near a set point. A sensor detects a variable, an integrator compares it with the set point, and effectors respond. Negative feedback reverses the change; positive feedback amplifies it and is rarer.

Regulators hold a variable steady; conformers let it follow the environment. A lizard is a conformer for body temperature; a sweating mammal is a regulator. Endothermy, warming the body by metabolism, costs energy.

sections.heading: Signals and muscles
sections.text:
Neurons carry electrical signals. The resting potential is negative inside, set mainly by potassium leak. An action potential is a brief reversal caused by sodium entry, then potassium exit. At a synapse, calcium entry releases neurotransmitter.

The endocrine system uses hormones, chemical messengers acting on distant targets; responses are slower but longer lasting. Muscles shorten when myosin heads pull actin filaments, powered by ATP, the cell’s energy carrier, and triggered by calcium. Skeletal muscle is striated (striped) and voluntary (consciously controlled); smooth is not striated and involuntary; cardiac is striated and involuntary.

sections.heading: Circulation and respiration
sections.text:
Circulatory systems may be open, with haemolymph bathing tissues, or closed, with blood in vessels. Fish have a single circuit; birds and mammals a double circuit. Respiratory surfaces are thin, moist and large.

Fish gills use countercurrent exchange: water and blood flow in opposite directions, keeping a gradient along the gill. The Fick principle: oxygen uptake equals cardiac output times arteriovenous oxygen difference. Example: output 5 L/min and difference 40 mL/L give 5 × 40 = 200 mL/min.

sections.heading: Excretion, digestion, reproduction
sections.text:
Excretion removes nitrogenous waste and controls water and salts. Aquatic animals often excrete ammonia, mammals urea, birds and insects uric acid.

Digestion may be intracellular or extracellular; animals have regional guts with enzymes. Reproduction may be asexual or sexual, with external or internal fertilisation. Oviparous animals lay eggs; viviparous animals develop young inside the mother. Freshwater tilapia drink little and excrete dilute urine; marine fish drink and excrete concentrated salts.

keyPoints: Homeostasis uses sensors, integrators and effectors; negative feedback reverses change, while positive feedback amplifies it.
Regulators hold internal variables steady, conformers let them follow the environment, and endothermy is metabolically costly.
Neurons signal by resting and action potentials; synapses release neurotransmitters, and hormones are slower blood-borne messengers.
Muscle contraction uses ATP and calcium to slide myosin and actin filaments; skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle differ in striation and control.
Open and closed circulatory systems, single and double circuits, and countercurrent gill exchange illustrate comparative transport.
The Fick principle states that oxygen uptake = cardiac output × arteriovenous oxygen difference.

en.title: Developmental biology
en.short: From fertilisation to organogenesis: differentiation, morphogenesis, genes and model organisms.

sections.heading: Fertilisation and cleavage
sections.text: Fertilisation is the fusion of a sperm and an egg to form a diploid zygote. It restores the chromosome number and activates development. In many animals, calcium waves block polyspermy (entry by more than one sperm) and start cleavage. Cleavage is a series of rapid mitotic divisions without growth, so the embryo divides into smaller cells called blastomeres. The pattern depends on yolk: holoblastic cleavage divides the whole egg (sea urchin, frog), while meroblastic cleavage divides only the cytoplasm-rich disc (bird, reptile). The result is a blastula.

sections.heading: Gastrulation and organogenesis
sections.text: Gastrulation rearranges the blastula into three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. Cells move by invagination, involution, ingression or epiboly. The ectoderm forms skin and nervous system, mesoderm forms muscle, bone and blood, and endoderm lines the gut and gives rise to liver and lungs. Organogenesis follows: the germ layers interact to form organs. Induction is a key mechanism: one group of cells signals another to change fate. In the classic Spemann and Mangold experiment, the dorsal lip of a newt blastopore transplanted to the ventral side induced a second body axis.

sections.heading: Differentiation and morphogenesis
sections.text: Cell differentiation is the process by which cells acquire specialised structures and functions, usually by differential gene expression. All cells have the same DNA, but different genes are switched on. Morphogenesis is the generation of shape through cell division, movement, adhesion and programmed cell death (apoptosis). A morphogen is a signalling molecule that forms a concentration gradient and specifies cell fate according to its concentration. Examples include retinoic acid and Sonic hedgehog.

sections.heading: Genes and model organisms
sections.text: Developmental genetics studies how genes control development. Maternal effect genes set up the egg axes; segmentation genes divide the Drosophila embryo into segments; Hox genes give each segment its identity along the head-to-tail axis. Model organisms are species chosen for easy study and shared developmental mechanisms: Drosophila, Xenopus, zebrafish, chick, mouse, Caenorhabditis elegans and Arabidopsis. Findings in one model often apply to others, including humans, but not always.

keyPoints: Fertilisation restores diploidy and activates the egg; cleavage divides the zygote into blastomeres without growth.
Gastrulation forms ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm, the three germ layers.
Organogenesis depends on induction, where one tissue signals another to change fate.
Differentiation is differential gene expression; morphogenesis is shape change by movement, adhesion and apoptosis.
Maternal effect, segmentation and Hox genes pattern the embryo along its axes.
Model organisms such as Drosophila, Xenopus, zebrafish and mouse reveal conserved developmental mechanisms.

en.title: Immunology: host defence and immune disorders
en.short: Innate and adaptive immunity, antibodies, T and B cells, MHC, complement, vaccines and immune disorders.

sections.heading: Two layers of defence
sections.text: Innate immunity is the fast, non-specific first line: physical barriers such as skin and mucus, phagocytes, inflammation and natural killer cells. It has no memory. Adaptive immunity is slower, specific and retains memory through lymphocytes. An antigen is any molecule recognised by an immune receptor; an epitope is the part actually bound. B cells make antibodies, while T cells help other cells or kill infected ones.

sections.heading: Antibodies and B cells
sections.text: An antibody, or immunoglobulin, is a Y-shaped protein with two variable antigen-binding sites. Binding can neutralise a toxin, clump microbes or mark them for phagocytosis. The constant region recruits phagocytes. A B cell carries a membrane antibody as its receptor. When it binds antigen and receives a helper T cell signal, it divides into plasma cells that secrete antibody and memory B cells.

sections.heading: T cells and MHC
sections.text: T cells recognise antigen fragments displayed on major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules. MHC I occurs on nearly all nucleated cells and presents peptides from inside the cell to CD8 cytotoxic T cells, which kill infected cells. MHC II occurs on antigen-presenting cells and presents peptides from outside the cell to CD4 helper T cells, which release chemical signals called cytokines. Clonal selection expands only lymphocytes whose receptors match the antigen.

sections.heading: Complement, vaccines, disorders
sections.text: Complement is a cascade of plasma proteins that enhances phagocytosis, lyses microbes and drives inflammation. Vaccination exposes a safe antigen so memory lymphocytes form before natural infection. Allergy is an immunoglobulin E (IgE) response to a harmless antigen, such as pollen. Autoimmunity is an adaptive attack on self antigens. Immunodeficiency is a failure of one or more immune components. Example: after measles vaccination a child may have mild fever, but memory cells can prevent later disease; protection is high but not absolute.

keyPoints: Innate immunity is fast and non-specific; adaptive immunity is slower, specific and has memory.
Antibodies are Y-shaped immunoglobulins that bind antigen and recruit other defences.
B cells become plasma cells that secrete antibody and memory B cells.
T cells recognise peptide fragments on MHC molecules; CD8 cells kill infected cells and CD4 cells help.
Complement is a plasma protein cascade that enhances phagocytosis, lysis and inflammation.
Vaccination builds memory safely; allergy, autoimmunity and immunodeficiency are failures or misdirections of immunity.

en.title: Ecology: populations, communities and ecosystems
en.short: Population growth models, species interactions, succession, ecosystem flows and biodiversity field methods.

sections.heading: Population dynamics
sections.text:
Population size N changes through births, deaths, immigration and emigration. Unlimited growth is exponential: dN/dt = rN, where r is the per capita growth rate. With carrying capacity K, logistic growth is dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K); growth is fastest at N = K/2.

Real populations vary with age and space. Life tables summarise age-specific survival; metapopulations are local populations linked by dispersal.

sections.heading: Interactions and succession
sections.text:
Species interactions include competition, predation, herbivory, parasitism, mutualism and facilitation. Competition may be exploitative or interference; competitive exclusion says two species cannot coexist indefinitely on the same limiting resource if niches overlap completely. Predation can regulate prey; Lotka-Volterra models describe coupled predator and prey dynamics.

Communities assemble through colonisation, extinction and environmental filtering. Succession is directional change after disturbance: primary succession starts on bare substrate, secondary succession follows where soil remains. Early species alter conditions and may be replaced; climax is not one fixed endpoint everywhere.

sections.heading: Ecosystem flows
sections.text:
Energy enters most ecosystems as light and is lost as heat at each transfer. Trophic efficiency is often about 10 per cent but varies, so food chains are short. Net primary production is gross primary production minus respiration.

Carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus cycle between organisms and the abiotic environment; nitrogen fixation, decomposition and weathering are key processes. Energy flows one way; matter is recycled.

sections.heading: Measuring biodiversity
sections.text:
Species richness counts species; evenness compares their abundances. The Shannon index is H = −Σ pi ln pi, where pi is the proportion of individuals in species i.

Field methods include quadrats for sessile organisms, transects for gradients and mark-recapture for mobile animals. In mark-recapture, N = (M × C) ÷ R, where M are marked, C are caught later and R are marked recaptures.

Example: M = 40, C = 50, R = 10, so N = (40 × 50) ÷ 10 = 200. This assumes a closed population, no mark loss and equal catchability.

keyPoints: Exponential growth is dN/dt = rN; logistic growth is dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), fastest at N = K/2.
Competitive exclusion and Lotka-Volterra models describe species interactions and coexistence limits.
Primary succession begins on bare substrate; secondary succession follows disturbance where soil remains.
Energy flows one way and is lost as heat; nutrients such as carbon and nitrogen are recycled.
Shannon diversity is H = −Σ pi ln pi, where pi is the proportion of species i.
Mark-recapture estimates N = (M × C) ÷ R under a closed population and equal catchability.

en.title: Conservation biology: biodiversity, threats and management
en.short: Biodiversity values, extinction risk, conservation genetics, protected areas, restoration, sustainable use and policy.

sections.heading: Biodiversity and threats
sections.text: Biodiversity is the variety of genes, species and ecosystems. It has intrinsic value and instrumental values such as use, option, bequest and existence. Main threats are habitat loss and fragmentation, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution and climate change. Small populations can enter an extinction vortex: genetic drift (random allele change), inbreeding depression and random events reduce fitness and numbers. The IUCN Red List ranks extinction risk from Least Concern to Extinct using population size, decline and range. Check Red List.

sections.heading: Conservation genetics
sections.text: Conservation genetics protects genetic diversity, which supports adaptation and avoids inbreeding depression. Drift fixes alleles faster in small populations. Effective population size Ne is the size of an ideal population with the same drift rate, often below census count. For Nm males and Nf females, Ne = 4NmNf ÷ (Nm + Nf). Expected loss of heterozygosity per generation is 1 ÷ (2Ne). Example: 10 male and 10 female breeders give Ne = 4 × 10 × 10 ÷ 20 = 20, so loss is 1 ÷ 40 = 0.025, or 2.5% per generation. A minimum viable population estimates the size needed to persist for a set time; it depends on species and model.

sections.heading: Protected areas and restoration
sections.text: Protected areas are managed spaces for conservation. Large, connected areas with buffer zones conserve more species than isolated fragments. Effectiveness depends on enforcement, funding and local support. Habitat restoration aims to return a degraded site to a reference ecosystem. It starts by removing the stressor, then replanting native species and monitoring. Restoration is slow and uncertain. A case is restoring a cleared mangrove creek by replanting and restoring tidal flow, then monitoring.

sections.heading: Sustainable use and policy
sections.text: Sustainable use takes resources without reducing renewal capacity. Maximum sustainable yield is the harvest keeping a population at its fastest growth, but management needs data and precaution. Policy works at several levels. The Convention on Biological Diversity and CITES are international agreements; national laws and community rules vary by country. Policy succeeds with local participation, clear rights and monitoring.

keyPoints: Biodiversity has intrinsic and instrumental value; main threats are habitat loss, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution and climate change.
The IUCN Red List assesses extinction risk using population size, decline and range criteria.
Effective population size is Ne = 4NmNf ÷ (Nm + Nf), and expected heterozygosity loss per generation is 1 ÷ (2Ne).
Small populations risk an extinction vortex through genetic drift and inbreeding depression.
Protected areas work best when large, connected and well managed with local support.
Sustainable use and conservation policy need data, precaution, clear rights and monitoring.

en.title: Evolutionary biology and phylogenetics
en.short: Microevolution, speciation, macroevolution, sexual selection, coevolution, molecular evolution and phylogenetic trees.

sections.heading: Microevolution and adaptation
sections.text: Microevolution is change in allele frequencies within a population. Mutation creates new alleles (gene variants); natural selection favours heritable variants that raise fitness (expected reproductive success); genetic drift is random change, strongest in small populations; gene flow moves alleles between populations. Adaptation is a heritable trait that improves survival or reproduction in a particular environment. Sexual selection is a form of natural selection acting on mating success. It works through competition within a sex or choice by the other sex, and can explain costly ornaments and sexual dimorphism.

sections.heading: Speciation and macroevolution
sections.text: A species is often defined by reproductive isolation (biological species concept), but morphological and phylogenetic concepts are also used. Speciation is the origin of new species, usually through reproductive isolation. Allopatric speciation follows geographic separation; sympatric speciation occurs without it, for example through polyploidy (extra chromosome sets) or host shifts. Macroevolution is evolution above the species level: speciation, extinction and adaptive radiation (rapid diversification). Patterns may be gradual or punctuated; both are debated for particular lineages.

sections.heading: Coevolution and molecules
sections.text: Coevolution is reciprocal selection between species, as in host and parasite or plant and pollinator. Molecular evolution studies changes in DNA and proteins. The neutral theory holds that much molecular variation is neutral, and that many substitutions are fixed by drift rather than selection. Molecular clocks use roughly steady substitution rates to date splits, but rates vary. Signals of selection can be detected by comparing amino-acid-changing and silent changes.

sections.heading: Phylogenetic trees
sections.text: A phylogenetic tree shows shared ancestry. Tips are taxa, nodes are common ancestors, and branch lengths may show time or change. Homology is similarity from common ancestry; analogy is convergence. Parsimony chooses the tree with fewest character changes; maximum likelihood and Bayesian methods use probabilistic models. An outgroup (a close relative outside the group) roots the tree. Read relationships by nodes: ((A,B),C) means A and B share a more recent ancestor with each other than with C. Tip order can be rotated without changing relationships.

keyPoints: Microevolution is change in allele frequencies caused by mutation, selection, drift and gene flow.
Sexual selection acts on mating success and can produce costly ornaments and sexual dimorphism.
Speciation is the origin of new species, usually through reproductive isolation; allopatric and sympatric modes are common.
Macroevolution covers speciation, extinction and adaptive radiation above the species level.
Coevolution is reciprocal selection between species; molecular clocks date splits but rates vary.
In a phylogenetic tree, relatedness is read from shared nodes, not from tip order.

en.title: Biotechnology: recombinant DNA and gene editing
en.short: Recombinant DNA, vectors, PCR, sequencing, gene editing and applications with biosafety.

sections.heading: Recombinant DNA and vectors
sections.text: Recombinant DNA technology joins DNA from different sources. Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences, often leaving sticky ends (single-stranded overhangs); DNA ligase seals the backbone. A cloning vector carries the insert into a host cell. Plasmids are small circular DNA molecules that replicate independently in bacteria. A vector needs an origin of replication, a selectable marker such as an antibiotic-resistance gene, and a cloning site. Bacteriophages, cosmids, bacterial artificial chromosomes (BACs) and yeast artificial chromosomes (YACs) carry larger inserts. Transformation introduces the vector into a host, often Escherichia coli; selection and screening identify successful uptake.

sections.heading: PCR and DNA sequencing
sections.text: PCR copies a defined DNA segment in vitro. Each cycle has denaturation (heat separates strands), annealing (primers bind), and extension (a thermostable DNA polymerase, commonly Taq, synthesises new strands). With perfect efficiency, copies = initial × 2^n. Example: one molecule after 20 cycles gives 2^20 = 1,048,576 copies; real efficiency is lower. Sanger sequencing uses dideoxynucleotides that stop chain extension, producing fragments of different lengths; capillary electrophoresis reads their order. Next-generation sequencing reads millions of fragments in parallel.

sections.heading: Gene editing
sections.text: Gene editing changes a specific DNA sequence. CRISPR-Cas9 uses a guide RNA complementary to a target and the Cas9 nuclease, which cuts both DNA strands. The cell repairs the break by non-homologous end joining, which often disrupts the gene, or by homology-directed repair, which can insert a chosen sequence if a template is supplied. Zinc finger nucleases and TALENs are earlier programmable nucleases. Off-target cuts are a main safety concern, so guide design and validation matter.

sections.heading: Applications and biosafety
sections.text: Medicine uses recombinant human insulin from bacteria or yeast, vaccines and gene therapy. Agriculture grows genetically modified crops with pest resistance or herbicide tolerance; traits and regulation differ by country. Industry uses engineered enzymes in detergents, fermentation products and biofuels. Biosafety means risk assessment and containment: laboratory practices, equipment and facility design matched to the organism’s risk group. National rules vary; the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety governs transboundary movement of living modified organisms.

keyPoints: Restriction enzymes cut DNA and DNA ligase joins it; cloning vectors carry inserts into host cells.
A plasmid vector needs an origin of replication, a selectable marker and a cloning site.
PCR cycles are denaturation, annealing and extension; copies = initial × 2^n at perfect efficiency.
Sanger sequencing uses chain-terminating dideoxynucleotides; next-generation sequencing reads many fragments in parallel.
CRISPR-Cas9 cuts a target DNA sequence guided by RNA; repair can disrupt or replace a gene.
Biosafety uses risk assessment and containment, and rules vary by country.

en.title: Bioinformatics
en.short: Databases, alignment and BLAST, phylogenetic trees, genome annotation and computational tools.

sections.heading: Biological databases
sections.text:
A biological database stores sequences, structures or annotations in a form a computer can search. Primary databases hold raw data deposited by researchers: GenBank (NCBI, USA), ENA (Europe) and DDBJ (Japan) share nucleotide sequences; UniProt holds proteins; the PDB holds three-dimensional structures.

Secondary databases add curation, such as Pfam and KEGG. Records carry accession numbers, which identify an entry, and versions, which change when the entry is updated. Record accession, version and date, because entries change.

sections.heading: Alignment and searching
sections.text:
Sequence alignment places two or more sequences side by side so that homologous (descended from a common ancestor) positions line up. Pairwise alignment may be global (Needleman-Wunsch, whole length) or local (Smith-Waterman, best region). It uses a scoring scheme: matches gain points, mismatches and gaps lose points. Similarity searching, usually with BLAST, compares a query against a database and reports hits with an E-value, the expected number of chance hits of that score or better in a database of that size. Small E-values suggest real matches.

Example: align ACGTACGT with ACGTTCGT. There are 7 matches and 1 mismatch in 8 positions. With match +1 and mismatch −1, score = 7 − 1 = 6. Identity = 7 ÷ 8 = 87.5%.

sections.heading: Trees and annotation
sections.text:
Phylogenetic analysis builds a tree from aligned sequences. Distance methods such as neighbour-joining compute pairwise distances then cluster; character methods such as maximum likelihood score possible trees under a model of substitution. Bootstrap resampling repeats the analysis on resampled columns; a bootstrap value near 100 means the clade is robust in that dataset.

Genome annotation finds genes and assigns functions. It predicts open reading frames (ORFs, the stretches between a start and a stop codon), splice sites and regulatory regions, then transfers function by homology to known genes. Automatic annotation is error-prone; review matters.

sections.heading: Computational tools
sections.text:
Tools range from web servers to command-line programs and scripts in Python or R. Reproducible work records versions, parameters and input files.

Check results against a positive control and note that databases contain errors and bias.

keyPoints: Primary databases (GenBank, ENA, DDBJ, UniProt, PDB) hold raw data; secondary databases add curation.
Global alignment covers whole sequences; local alignment finds the best matching region.
BLAST reports an E-value, the expected number of chance hits; smaller values are more significant.
With match +1 and mismatch −1, alignment score = matches − mismatches, and identity = matches ÷ alignment length.
Phylogenetic trees use distance or character methods; bootstrap values test clade support.
Genome annotation predicts ORFs and transfers function by homology; automatic calls need review.

en.title: Laboratory and field methods in biology
en.short: Core lab and field techniques, from microscopy to sampling, recording and safety.

sections.heading: Microscopy and sterility
sections.text:
Microscopy uses lenses to magnify small objects. Resolution, the smallest distance at which two points are seen as separate, depends mainly on wavelength and numerical aperture (a measure of how much light the lens can gather), not only magnification. Light microscopes suit living cells; electron microscopes give higher resolution but need fixed, dehydrated specimens.

Aseptic technique keeps cultures and sterile media free from unwanted microbes: work near a flame or in a laminar-flow hood (a cabinet supplied with filtered air), flame loops, use sterile containers and never touch sterile surfaces.

sections.heading: Measuring and separating
sections.text:
Spectrophotometry measures how much light a solution absorbs. The Beer-Lambert law is A = εcl, where A is absorbance, ε the molar absorption coefficient, c concentration and l path length.

Example: ε = 15,000 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, c = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L, l = 1 cm, so A = 15,000 × 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 1 = 0.30.

Chromatography separates molecules by their different movement between a mobile phase (moving fluid) and a stationary phase (fixed material). Electrophoresis separates charged molecules, such as DNA or proteins, through a gel under an electric field; smaller molecules, or those with more charge for their size, move faster.

sections.heading: Sampling and surveys
sections.text:
Biological sampling must be representative and unbiased. Random sampling gives every unit a known chance of selection; stratified sampling divides the population into groups first. Record sample size, location, date and method.

Field surveys may use quadrats for plants, transects along a gradient, or capture-recapture for mobile animals. Capture-recapture estimates population size N as (M × C) ÷ R, where M are marked, C caught second time and R marked recaptures. This assumes marks are not lost and the population is closed.

sections.heading: Records and safety
sections.text:
Record data at the time of collection in a bound notebook or secure file: raw readings, units, instrument settings and any deviations. Label samples uniquely.

Laboratory safety includes risk assessment, correct waste disposal, gloves and goggles, and knowing emergency procedures. Field safety includes telling others your plan, checking weather and carrying first aid. Rules differ by institution and country; follow local training and official guidance.

keyPoints: Resolution, not magnification alone, limits what a microscope can show.
Aseptic technique protects sterile media and cultures from contamination.
Beer-Lambert law: A = εcl; check units before calculating concentration.
Chromatography separates by distribution between mobile and stationary phases; electrophoresis separates charged molecules in an electric field.
Representative sampling and capture-recapture formula N = (M × C) ÷ R depend on stated assumptions.
Record raw data, units and settings at once, and follow local safety rules.

en.title: Biology ethics, biosafety and professional practice
en.short: Covers research ethics, consent, human and animal approval, biosafety levels, GMO rules, data integrity and plagiarism.

sections.heading: Research ethics
sections.text: Research ethics is the principles that keep biological work honest and protect people, animals and the public.
