Core duties are honesty, respect, beneficence and non-maleficence (do good and avoid harm), justice and accountability. Informed consent means a competent person freely agrees after clear information about purpose, procedures, risks, benefits and the right to withdraw. A signature alone is not enough if the person did not understand. For children, a guardian usually gives permission and the child gives assent. Legal details vary by country.

sections.heading: Human and animal approval
sections.text: Human research needs approval from an independent ethics committee, often an institutional review board (IRB), before data or samples are collected. Animal research needs approval from an animal care and use committee. Scientists must justify animal use and apply the 3Rs: replacement, reduction and refinement. Committee names and laws vary by country, so check your institution and national regulator. Case: a student in Ghana plans a patient survey and a rat experiment. She needs both approvals, consent forms and supervisor sign-off before starting.

sections.heading: Biosafety levels
sections.text: Biosafety means containing biological agents so workers, the public and the environment are protected. BSL1 is low-risk work with standard microbiological practice. BSL2 adds restricted access, protective clothing and controlled waste for moderate risk. BSL3 adds negative air pressure and stricter entry for agents that can cause serious disease. BSL4 uses full containment for the most dangerous agents. National rules assign agents to levels; workers must follow them.

sections.heading: GMOs and integrity
sections.text: Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) are organisms altered by genetic engineering. Many countries regulate them through risk assessment, approval and monitoring, but laws differ; Nigeria’s National Biosafety Management Agency handles approvals. Data integrity means data are complete, accurate and traceable. Keep raw data and dated records, and never fabricate or falsify results. Plagiarism is presenting another person’s words, ideas, images or data as your own; cite sources and follow institutional policy. Responsibilities include safe practice, honest reporting, fair authorship and reporting misconduct.

keyPoints: Research ethics protects participants and keeps science honest; informed consent must be voluntary, informed and documented.
Human studies need independent ethics approval; animal studies need animal care and use approval and the 3Rs.
Biosafety levels 1 to 4 match containment to risk, and national rules assign agents to levels.
GMO work is usually regulated nationally, so check the current law and approval process.
Data integrity requires complete, accurate, traceable records; never fabricate or falsify results.
Plagiarism is using others’ words, ideas, images or data without acknowledgement; cite sources and follow policy.

en.title: The undergraduate research project and scientific communication
en.short: Planning a supervised project, searching literature, analysing data, writing, referencing and presenting.

sections.heading: Planning the project
sections.text:
A supervised project starts with a narrow, answerable question and a realistic plan. Meet your supervisor early, agree the question, the methods, the timeline and the ethics or safety approvals your institution requires. Keep a dated laboratory or field notebook and back up raw data.

Case: Amina, a final-year student in Kano, plans a project on how shade affects bean growth. She limits the study to one variety, three shade levels and six weeks, because that fits her time and equipment. Her supervisor helps her check feasibility.

sections.heading: Searching the literature
sections.text:
A literature search finds what is already known and shows the gap your project fills. Use your library’s databases and Google Scholar. Combine search terms with Boolean operators: AND narrows, OR widens, NOT excludes. Record the databases, dates and search strings you use, and save PDFs with full details.

Primary papers report original data; reviews summarise a field. Read the abstract first, then the methods and results. Take notes in your own words and note the page or paragraph for each idea.

sections.heading: Analysing and writing
sections.text:
Data analysis means organising, checking, summarising and interpreting your data. Keep a tidy table with clear variable names and units. Use a spreadsheet or software such as R, Python or SPSS, and keep the raw file unchanged.

Scientific writing usually follows IMRaD: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion, with a title, abstract and references. Write plainly, use past tense for what you did, and give each figure or table a caption. Referencing must follow your department’s style, such as APA, Harvard or Vancouver. Cite every idea that is not your own, even when paraphrased; copying without acknowledgement is plagiarism.

sections.heading: Presenting your work
sections.text: A poster should make one clear message. Use a large title, readable text, simple figures and a short spoken summary of one to three minutes. An oral presentation needs timed slides, practice and preparation for questions. In both, explain why the question matters, what you did, what you found and what it means.

keyPoints: Plan a narrow, feasible question with your supervisor before collecting data.
Use Boolean operators and record your search strategy and sources.
Keep raw data unchanged and analyse a tidy, labelled copy.
Write in IMRaD structure and cite every borrowed idea in the required style.
A poster carries one message; an oral talk needs timing and practice.

en.title: Advanced cell signalling and molecular biology
en.short: Signal transduction, receptor classes, second messengers, chromatin, gene networks and current methods.

sections.heading: Signal transduction and receptors
sections.text:
Signal transduction converts an extracellular cue into a response. Ligand binding activates receptors, then kinases add phosphate groups and GTPases such as Ras switch between GTP-bound active and GDP-bound inactive states. Scaffold proteins organise pathways and improve specificity.

Receptor classes include G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), which activate heterotrimeric G proteins; receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), which dimerise and autophosphorylate; ionotropic receptors, which are ligand-gated ion channels; and nuclear receptors, which regulate transcription.

For simple binding, occupancy θ = [L] ÷ (Kd + [L]). If Kd = 10 nM and [L] = 30 nM, θ = 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75, so 75% of receptors are occupied.

sections.heading: Second messengers
sections.text: Second messengers are small intracellular molecules that relay a signal. cAMP, made by adenylyl cyclase and broken down by phosphodiesterase, activates protein kinase A. IP3 releases Ca²⁺ from the endoplasmic reticulum, and DAG activates protein kinase C. Ca²⁺, cGMP and PIP3 are other messengers. One receptor can generate many messenger molecules, so the signal is amplified; the exact gain varies by cell and pathway.

sections.heading: Chromatin and gene networks
sections.text:
Chromatin is DNA wrapped around histone octamers into nucleosomes. Histone acetylation usually loosens chromatin, while histone methylation can activate or repress depending on the residue. DNA methylation at CpG sites is often repressive. Remodellers move nucleosomes, and enhancers contact promoters through loops inside topologically associating domains.

A gene regulatory network (GRN) is a set of genes, proteins and regulatory links. Motifs such as feed-forward loops filter noise, and positive feedback can produce bistability, meaning two stable states. GRNs help explain how transcription factors pattern tissues.

sections.heading: Experimental approaches
sections.text: Current methods include CRISPR screens to test gene function at scale, single-cell RNA sequencing to measure transcripts per cell, ATAC-seq for open chromatin, and ChIP-seq or CUT&RUN for binding sites. Live-cell FRET biosensors and optogenetics probe signalling in real time. Phosphoproteomics maps phosphorylation sites, and proximity labelling maps protein interactions. Results need controls, replication and independent validation.

keyPoints: Signal transduction relies on receptor activation, phosphorylation and GTPase switches.
Main receptor classes are GPCRs, RTKs, ionotropic receptors and nuclear receptors.
Receptor occupancy for simple binding is θ = [L] ÷ (Kd + [L]).
cAMP, Ca²⁺, IP3, DAG and PIP3 are second messengers that amplify and diversify signals.
Chromatin state is set by histone modification, DNA methylation, remodelling and enhancer loops.
Gene regulatory networks use motifs and feedback to produce robust or bistable responses; CRISPR screens, single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq are key current methods.

en.title: Advanced ecology and evolutionary biology
en.short: Population and community theory, quantitative and molecular evolution, and ecological modelling.

sections.heading: Population and community theory
sections.text: The logistic model dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K) adds density dependence to exponential growth; r is the intrinsic rate of increase and K the carrying capacity. In two-species competition, dN1/dt = r1N1(1 − (N1 + α12N2)/K1), where α12 is the competitive effect of species 2 on species 1. Coexistence requires α12 < K1/K2 and α21 < K2/K1. Community theory asks how niches, dispersal and disturbance allow species to persist without competitive exclusion.

sections.heading: Quantitative and evolutionary genetics
sections.text: Quantitative genetics separates phenotypic variance VP into additive genetic VA, dominance, epistasis and environmental VE. Narrow-sense heritability h² = VA/VP predicts response to selection by the breeder’s equation R = h²S, where S is the selection differential. Example: h² = 0.4 and S = 2.5 g give R = 0.4 × 2.5 = 1.0 g per generation. In population genetics, allele frequencies change under selection, mutation, drift and migration; drift is strong when the effective population size Ne is small.

sections.heading: Molecular evolution
sections.text: Molecular evolution compares DNA and protein sequences. Synonymous substitutions do not change the amino acid; non-synonymous substitutions do. The ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous substitution rates, ω = dN/dS, measures selection: ω < 1 suggests purifying selection, ω = 1 neutrality, and ω > 1 positive selection. Neutral theory holds that most molecular substitutions are neutral and fix at rate μ, the mutation rate. Coalescent theory traces gene copies backward to common ancestors; it underlies estimates of Ne and demographic history.

sections.heading: Modelling and conservation
sections.text: Models make assumptions explicit. Matrix models project age- or stage-structured populations as n(t+1) = A n(t); the dominant eigenvalue λ gives asymptotic growth (λ > 1 means increase). Population viability analysis uses such models with stochasticity to estimate extinction risk. Occupancy models separate presence from detection probability. Example: logistic growth with r = 0.5 per year, K = 1000, N = 100 gives dN/dt = 0.5 × 100 × (1 − 100/1000) = 45 individuals per year. Always check units, uncertainty and model assumptions.

keyPoints: Logistic growth is dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), and two-species coexistence requires α12 < K1/K2 and α21 < K2/K1.
Narrow-sense heritability is h² = VA/VP, and the predicted selection response is R = h²S.
The dN/dS ratio ω indicates purifying selection when below 1, neutrality at 1 and positive selection above 1.
Neutral theory predicts a molecular substitution rate equal to the mutation rate μ.
Matrix models use n(t+1) = A n(t), with asymptotic growth given by the dominant eigenvalue λ.
Model results depend on assumptions, units and uncertainty, so check them against data and theory.

en.title: Systems biology and advanced bioinformatics
en.short: Analysing omics data, inferring networks and building computational models of biological systems.

sections.heading: Omics data
sections.text:
Genomics studies DNA sequence and variation. Transcriptomics measures RNA abundance, proteomics measures proteins and metabolomics measures small molecules. These data are high-dimensional, noisy and affected by batch effects, which are technical differences between batches of samples processed separately. Preprocessing therefore matters: normalise between samples, filter low-quality features, log-transform skewed values and impute missing values only with care.

Differential analysis compares groups. A gene with normalised counts 100 in control and 400 in treated has log2 fold change log2(400 ÷ 100) = 2, meaning fourfold higher. Because thousands of features are tested, control the false discovery rate (FDR), the expected proportion of false positives among declared discoveries.

sections.heading: Statistical analysis
sections.text:
Clustering groups samples or genes with similar profiles. Principal component analysis (PCA) reduces many features to a few axes that capture major variation, often revealing batch structure. Supervised machine learning predicts labels from features, but needs cross-validation and an independent test set to avoid overfitting.

Advanced methods include batch correction, network inference and multi-omics integration. Results should be reproducible: record versions, parameters and code.

sections.heading: Networks and models
sections.text:
A network represents molecules as nodes and relationships as edges, such as protein interactions or gene regulation. Degree is the number of edges at a node; centrality ranks influential nodes. A star network with one hub joined to four leaves has degrees 4,1,1,1,1, so mean degree = 8 ÷ 5 = 1.6.

Dynamic models use ordinary differential equations to describe changing concentrations. Constraint-based metabolic models use flux balance analysis to predict steady-state fluxes. Systems biology combines these models with omics data, but predictions must be tested experimentally.

sections.heading: Limits and integration
sections.text: Multi-omics integration can reveal mechanisms that one layer misses, but scale differences, missing data and confounding make it difficult. Treat computational findings as hypotheses until validated. Check current standards and repositories for data sharing.

keyPoints: Genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics measure DNA, RNA, proteins and small molecules respectively.
Normalise, filter and log-transform omics data before comparison; control FDR when testing many features.
log2 fold change = log2(treated ÷ control); a value of 2 means fourfold higher.
PCA and clustering explore high-dimensional data; supervised models need cross-validation and independent test data.
Networks use nodes and edges; mean degree = 2 × edges ÷ nodes for an undirected network.
ODE models and flux balance analysis predict system behaviour, but computational predictions need experimental validation.

en.title: Research methods and dissertation in biology
en.short: Designing, analysing, writing and defending a master’s biology research project.

sections.heading: Design and review
sections.text:
Advanced research design means matching the design to the question. An experiment manipulates a factor with randomisation, replication and blocking to control confounding. An observational study, such as a cohort or case-control study, estimates associations without intervention. Before data collection, a power analysis sets the sample size.

A literature review is not a list of papers. A systematic review uses a written search strategy, clear inclusion criteria and critical appraisal, then synthesises findings. It reduces cherry-picking.

Example: to detect a 5 cm difference in mean plant height with standard deviation 10 cm, two-sided α = 0.05 and power 0.80, n per group = 2(1.96 + 0.84)² × 10² ÷ 5² = 63.

sections.heading: Proposal and ethics
sections.text: A proposal states the question, aims, hypotheses, methods, budget and timeline. Grant writing adds feasibility and fit with the funder’s priorities; justify every resource. Ethical approval comes before data collection. An ethics committee reviews consent, risk, confidentiality, animal welfare and biosafety. In many countries, human research also needs data protection compliance; check local rules.

sections.heading: Analysis and reproducibility
sections.text:
Choose the statistical model from the design and data type. Check assumptions, report effect sizes and confidence intervals, and correct for multiple comparisons. Do not change the hypothesis after seeing results; that is HARKing. Trying many analyses until one is significant is p-hacking.

Reproducibility means another researcher can obtain the same results from your data and code. Share protocols, metadata, analysis code and, where possible, data. Preregistration records the plan before data collection.

sections.heading: Writing and defence
sections.text:
A dissertation is an argument, not a lab diary. Structure it as introduction, methods, results, discussion and conclusion. Each figure and table must answer a question. The discussion states limitations and what the work adds.

In an oral defence or viva, you explain your choices, defend your analysis and show that you know the literature. Prepare a short summary, anticipate questions about design and statistics, and be honest about weaknesses.

keyPoints: Match the design to the question; use randomisation, replication and blocking to control confounding.
A power analysis before data collection sets the sample size; for two means, n per group = 2(z0.975 + z0.80)² × SD² ÷ difference² when α = 0.05 and power = 0.80.
A systematic literature review uses a written search strategy, inclusion criteria and critical appraisal.
Ethical approval from an ethics committee is needed before data collection; check local and institutional rules.
Report effect sizes and confidence intervals, correct for multiple comparisons, and avoid p-hacking.
Reproducibility requires shared protocols, metadata, code and data where possible; the viva defends your choices.
